questions.prompt: Which set of variables makes up the friendship formula in this chapter?
choices: Proximity, frequency, duration, and intensity
Warmth, honesty, confidence, and humor
Interest, similarity, trust, and loyalty

explanation.gentle: The chapter's model uses four variables: proximity, frequency, duration, and intensity.
explanation.direct: Schafer names four conditions, not four personality traits.
explanation.competitive: The chapter is built on a four-lever model, and option A is the actual set.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter say proximity is not enough by itself?
choices: Because nearness matters only when the setting feels nonthreatening and other variables support closeness
Because proximity works only in romantic relationships
Because physical distance never affects attachment

explanation.gentle: Nearness helps, but only when the atmosphere feels safe enough for openness and the relationship has more than simple access.
explanation.direct: Proximity is necessary in many cases, but it does little if threat stays high or the other variables stay weak.
explanation.competitive: Access is not attachment. If the conditions stay guarded, nearness does almost nothing.

questions.prompt: A teammate greets you every morning but never stays longer than ten seconds. Which variable is clearly present, and which one is clearly weak?
choices: Duration is present, frequency is weak
Frequency is present, duration is weak
Intensity is present, proximity is weak

explanation.gentle: Daily greetings create frequency, but the very short interaction keeps duration low.
explanation.direct: Repeated contact is high here, while time length is minimal.

questions.prompt: Maya sees Elias every day at work, but their talks stay rushed and forgettable. What would best improve the relationship according to the formula?
choices: Add more random interruptions so the frequency becomes overwhelming
Create slightly longer, warmer exchanges so duration and intensity improve
Stop talking altogether so the proximity becomes more noticeable

explanation.gentle: Her main problem is not lack of access. It is that the interaction is too brief and too flat to build closeness.
explanation.direct: The missing variables are duration and intensity, not raw proximity.
explanation.competitive: More noise is the trap. Better-weighted contact is the move.

questions.prompt: A study group meets four times a week but nobody feels close enough to ask real questions. Which reading fits the chapter best?
choices: The group has enough frequency, but likely lacks duration, safety, or intensity
The group should meet even more often and the problem will solve itself
The problem proves the formula does not apply outside personal friendships

explanation.gentle: Frequent meetings do not automatically create closeness if the time stays rushed or emotionally flat.
explanation.direct: This is a classic case of one variable looking strong while others remain weak.
explanation.competitive: Repetition without weight still produces a thin bond.

questions.prompt: Which statement captures the chapter's warning about duration?
choices: Longer relationships are always healthier than shorter ones
More duration can deepen the wrong bond as easily as the right one
Duration matters only after intensity disappears

explanation.gentle: The chapter warns that stronger attachment is not automatically good attachment.
explanation.direct: Duration can strengthen unhealthy influence too, which is why the formula is not moral proof.
explanation.competitive: More time is not automatically a gift. Sometimes it just digs the tie deeper.

questions.prompt: A remote mentorship starts fading even though the monthly check-in still happens. Which shift most likely explains the decline?
choices: Frequency stayed the same, but duration and intensity dropped
Proximity increased too much, which weakened the relationship
The formula stops working in remote settings

explanation.gentle: A relationship can weaken when the meeting remains on the calendar but loses time and emotional weight.
explanation.direct: The chapter applies across settings because it tracks conditions, not physical labels.
explanation.competitive: The bond is not dying because it is remote. It is dying because the important variables shrank.

questions.prompt: Leah wants distance from a draining classmate without a big confrontation. What fits the chapter best?
choices: Deliver a dramatic speech immediately, because lowering the variables never works
Quietly reduce proximity, frequency, duration, and intensity over time
Increase intensity first so the relationship ends on a stronger note

explanation.gentle: The formula works in reverse too, which means relationships often cool when the variables weaken.
explanation.direct: The chapter's practical insight is that attachment can lose momentum without theatrical rupture.
explanation.competitive: Do not feed the bond you want to shrink.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest ethical caution built into the friendship formula?
choices: Only extroverts can use it well
It explains how attachment grows, but not whether the bond is healthy or deserved
It works only when both people know the formula

explanation.gentle: The chapter leaves a real tension alive: growth conditions can be used well or badly.
explanation.direct: Schafer's model is descriptive and strategic, but it does not certify moral quality.
explanation.competitive: The map can show you how to deepen the tie. It cannot tell you the tie is worth deepening.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter naturally lead into a chapter about first impressions and friend signals?
choices: Because the formula matters only after a relationship has lasted several years
Because before the variables can build over time, someone has to feel safe enough to keep engaging
Because intensity becomes irrelevant once first impressions are discussed

explanation.gentle: The formula needs time and repeated contact, so the next question is what makes someone grant that early chance.
explanation.direct: Chapter 2 follows by explaining the low-threat opening signals that let relationship growth begin.
explanation.competitive: No formula can scale if the other person never gives you the first few safe seconds.
